title: Palindrome Partitioning
prompt:
Given a string `s`, partition it such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitionings of `s`.

For deterministic comparison, sort the outer list of partitions (for example, by converting each partition to a tuple and sorting the list of tuples).

examples.explanation: Both partitions split "aab" entirely into palindromic pieces.
The smallest possible input: a single character is trivially its own palindrome partition.
Every substring of an all-repeated-character string is a palindrome, so every possible cut pattern is valid.

constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters
hints: At every position in the string, you're choosing where to make the next cut — that's the branching decision for backtracking.
From the current start position, try every possible end position for the next piece; only recurse into it if that substring s[start:end] is itself a palindrome.

Since a palindrome check on the same substring may get repeated across branches, consider caching is_palindrome(i, j) results (memoization) to avoid rechecking, though for the given constraints a direct check per candidate substring is also fast enough.

solution.approach: Backtrack over cut positions: at each start index, try every possible end index for the next piece (start+1 up to len(s)), and only recurse further if s[start:end] is a palindrome — this prunes the search tree so we never build a partition containing a non-palindromic piece. When start reaches the end of the string, the current path is a complete valid partitioning, so record a copy. Checking palindromes with simple string reversal comparison is fine given the small input size; for larger inputs this could be sped up with a precomputed palindrome table or memoized checks.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) recursion depth, plus output size
